details:
AstroVitals is a web-based health monitoring system for astronauts on long-duration missions. It gives crew members a clear, visual picture of their own health and helps them decide when to act.

The astronaut app gathers vital signs (heart rate, SpO₂, respiratory rate, skin temperature) and shows them with color-coded status and trend charts. Each result is compared against the astronaut's own pre-flight baseline and clinical reference ranges for blood gases, cardiac enzymes, blood counts, lipids and iron. An interactive 3D spacesuit model lets astronauts click body regions, such as the eyes and heart, to see the exams and status for each. These target two key spaceflight risks: Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), tracked through OCT eye scans, and cardiovascular changes such as cardiac atrophy, tracked through cardiac ultrasound. An AI medical copilot answers questions using only built-in medical reference material, so astronauts don't need expert knowledge to understand their results.

What it does and how it works

AstroVitals combines a role-based web frontend with a FastAPI backend to support astronaut self-monitoring and medical oversight: Astronaut experience: Crew members can access a dashboard, monitoring views, baseline records, examinations, history, reports, settings, medical guidance, and an AI copilot. Vital signs are presented with color-coded status indicators and trend visualizations to make changes easier to interpret.

Personalized clinical context: Measurements and lab values are compared against each astronaut’s pre-flight baseline and clinical reference ranges (including blood gases, cardiac enzymes, blood counts, lipids, and iron) to provide individualized insight rather than generic thresholds alone.

3D spacesuit interaction: An interactive 3D spacesuit model lets astronauts select body regions (such as eyes and heart) to review related exams and health status. This links anatomy-focused exploration to mission-relevant risks like SANS (via OCT eye scans) and cardiovascular changes such as cardiac atrophy (via cardiac ultrasound).

AI medical copilot: The copilot helps astronauts understand results by answering questions using medical reference material, reducing the need for specialized medical expertise during routine interpretation.

Medical admin portal: A companion interface for flight surgeons/medical admins supports crew review, exam approvals/findings, calendar coordination, alerts, and shared reporting to maintain a unified view of astronaut health.The frontend is structured with a dedicated data/service layer so it can operate with placeholder data during development and connect to backend APIs through environment-configured endpoints. Benefits:Clear, actionable health visibility: Translates raw measurements into understandable visual summaries and status cues.Personalized interpretation: Uses pre-flight baselines and clinical ranges to highlight meaningful deviations for each astronaut.Faster awareness of mission-critical risks: Focuses attention on key spaceflight health concerns (SANS and cardiac changes) through targeted exams and region-based navigation.Improved collaboration: Gives astronauts and ground medical teams a shared view of findings, alerts, and reports.Accessible guidance: Helps non-experts interpret results through an AI copilot grounded in built-in medical references.

Impact: AstroVitals is designed to support early detection and informed decision-making for crews operating far from immediate medical care. By unifying monitoring, clinical context, and communication between astronauts and flight surgeons, the project aims to reduce response delays, improve situational awareness, and strengthen health management during long-duration missions.

Tools, Languages, and Software: Frontend: React, Vite, JavaScript/JSX, CSS . 3D & visualization: Three.js, @react-three/fiber, @react-three/drei, Recharts Backend/API: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn

Platform: Web-based applicationCreativity and Design ApproachAnatomy-driven interaction: The interactive 3D spacesuit provides an intuitive, spatial way to explore health data by body region instead of relying only on tables and menus.Human-centered health communication: Color-coded statuses, trends, and baseline comparisons are designed to make complex medical information easier to understand under mission constraints.Dual-role system in one platform: Separate astronaut and medical-admin interfaces share authentication/session concepts while addressing different workflows and responsibilities.AI-assisted understanding: The medical copilot focuses on explanation and accessibility, helping astronauts interpret results without replacing clinical oversight.Factors ConsideredLimited access to immediate medical support:** Interfaces prioritize clarity, early warning signals, and quick access to relevant information.Personal variability: Baseline-aware comparisons help account for individual differences between astronauts.Mission-relevant health risks: The project emphasizes SANS and cardiovascular changes as critical concerns in spaceflight.Usability and trust: Role-based access, structured navigation, and clear presentation support reliable use by both crew and medical teams. Integration readiness: A modular data/service architecture and configurable API endpoints were considered to support future backend connectivity and deployment.Safety in communication: The AI copilot is designed to rely on built-in medical reference material to provide consistent, explainable guidance.
